claim_11_6.evidence: Magnitude reproduces closely (mean_dce 0.00445 vs 0.00454, frac_gt_0.5 0.00331 vs 0.00467 -- both within ~30%, so the head really is narrow/small), but the QUALITATIVE category label does not survive a fresh sample: only 2 of 15 top-dCE fresh examples are people's-surname-after-given-name completions. The dominant pattern in fresh data is completing the SECOND token of any low-frequency, often Latin/botanical or otherwise unusual capitalized multi-token term -- 'helps rare multi-token proper nouns/technical terms in general' fits the fresh evidence at least as well as, arguably better than, 'roster-surname predictor'. This looks like a case of the wave-1 author writing a narrative that fit their particular 10-example sample (skip=900) and not checking it against a different sample.

claim_mlp1_category.original_claim: mlp1 = giant front token-table; scope is 'the next BPE fragment of an in-progress multi-token word or fixed phrase', not context-dependent selection at all
fresh_top10_examples_classified: ratification ... reform[ treaty] -- NOT a fragment: full recurring topic word, context-dependent recall
Third Planting of\n[Rich] -- NOT a fragment: predicts the START of a repeated proper-noun phrase from earlier context (copy/recency), not completion of an in-progress word
have the power to accept or reject this[ treaty] -- NOT a fragment: topic-word recall
Ratification of the[ treaty] -- NOT a fragment: topic-word recall
claim_mlp1_category.evidence: 6 of the top-10 fresh dCE positions are genuine mid-word BPE-fragment completions (Rich->boro x2, er->ode, instit->utes, constell->ations, Ock->endon), consistent with the claim. But 4/10 -- and the single highest-dCE example overall (30.65 nats, 'reform treaty') -- are NOT subword fragments at all: they are full, already-complete words ('treaty' x3, 'Rich' as a whole start-of-phrase token) that recur as the salient topic/proper-noun of THIS specific document. That is a document-level repetition/recency-recall mechanism, not 'the next BPE fragment of an in-progress word or fixed phrase' as claimed. The category story captures a real and large chunk of mlp1's behavior but omits an equally prominent failure mode (topical word repetition) that shows up as soon as the sample changes.

strongest_objection: The wave-1 workflow is structurally prone to gerrymandering: a category narrative is written from a single specificity_and_scope() call's top-10/30 examples (one skip value, one 96-row sample), then reported as 'the' scope of the circuit without ever re-sampling to see if the label survives. Concretely, head 11.6's 'roster-surname predictor' story falls apart on a fresh sample (2/15 genuine matches; the rest are botanical Latin binomials, bird names, and generic subwords), and even mlp1's well-established 'next-BPE-fragment' story -- the most robust, most-replicated claim in this whole wave -- turns out to omit a second, equally strong failure mode (document-topic-word repetition, e.g. 'treaty' recurring 5x in one sample) that a different skip immediately surfaces. Given that every one of the 9 records reused the SAME mlp1 scope_stats (mean_dce=8.35646, frac_gt_0.5=0.9439, n_positions=18432, skip=900, presumably cached and never independently re-verified per-datapoint), the wave-1 authors were pattern-matching against one fixed reference sample throughout, which is exactly the setup that produces narratives fit to noise. Recommendation: any circuit-category claim should be scope-tested against at least 2 disjoint skips before being written into a final record, and the mlp1 scope stats specifically should be refreshed rather than copy-pasted 9 times.
